bib.title: Runtime-Independent Persistent Agents: Preserving Identity, Memory, and Code Across Models, Harnesses, and Servers

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Runtime-Independent Persistent Agents: Preserving Identity, Memory, and Code Across Models, Harnesses, and Servers" (RIPA / Enoch), Zhenyu Zhao and Roy Zhao, independent researcher and Univ. of Washington. arXiv:2609.00546v2 [cs.SE], 19 Sep 2026, preprint. Reference implementation: github.com/our-ark/enoch.

COVERAGE: 51,339 of 51,339 chars read, including the references. The extraction is clean text with some words fused. I did not extract figures separately. Captions are quoted from the body text.

TYPE: A hybrid. It is mainly an architecture/design paper with a formal boundary, six invariants and a protocol. It also has a small empirical section: a few live case studies plus mechanism tests. It is not a benchmark and has no statistical results. The authors say they "do not estimate statistical reliability, operator burden, cost or model performance."

CLAIMS (ranked)
- The paper defines the persistent agent as a state triple (identity, memory, executable body), not as model plus harness. Model, harness and host are a replaceable execution substrate. Chats, APIs and email are replaceable interaction surfaces.
  number: none
  setup: definition, not measured
  quote: "P𝑡 = (𝐼𝑡 , 𝑀𝑡 , 𝐵𝑡 )" and "E𝑡 = (𝑅𝑡 , 𝐻𝑡 , 𝐷 𝑡 )" and "A𝑡 = P𝑡 ⊲ (E 𝑡 , S𝑡 )"
  where: Sec 2.1, p2
- "Model plus harness" answers only the synchronic question (what generates behavior now). It does not answer the diachronic one (what must stay continuous across time). This is the paper's critique of the standard agent definition.
  number: none
  quote: "A common shorthand identifies an agent with a model plus an agent harness. It captures a useful synchronic question: what currently generates behavior? It does not answer the diachronic question"
  where: Sec 1, p1
- State that persists across runs and runtimes is split as follows. M is private durable memory plus continuity-relevant workflow state. B is the versioned code, prompts, tools, policies, tests and provider contracts. I is the identity record. Queue state and task identity stay in the persistent substrate, not in a transient harness transcript. A transcript is raw evidence, not memory.
  number: none
  quote: "Queue state and task identity likewise remain in the persistent substrate, not in a transient harness transcript." and "A transcript is raw interaction evidence, not automatically memory"
  where: Sec 3.3, p4
- Session continuity differs from agent continuity. After migration a fresh harness session is expected, and context is rebuilt from durable state.
  number: none
  quote: "The agent reconstructs its context from identity, memory, body, and durable work records instead of treating one provider-native conversation as its mind."
  where: Sec 3.3, p4
- Continuity means lineage, not byte equality. A pure runtime migration keeps identity version and body revision fixed, and memory may only extend its ancestry.
  number: none
  quote: "𝑣 𝐼 (𝑡 + 1) = 𝑣 𝐼 (𝑡), 𝑣 𝑀 (𝑡) ⪯ 𝑣 𝑀 (𝑡 + 1), 𝑣 𝐵 (𝑡 + 1) = 𝑣 𝐵 (𝑡)"
  where: Sec 2.2, eq 5, p2
- Copying state does not copy authority. A stable name or UUID is insufficient, because a directory copied to two servers carries the same ID. Unique continuation needs a lease, fencing epoch or declared multi-embodiment policy.
  number: none
  quote: "Agent continuity requires identity, attributable lineage, and transition authority; a stable label alone is insufficient."
  where: Sec 2.3, p2; Sec 7.2, p9
- The paper names seven lifecycle operations: restart, resume, migrate, evolve, identity update, replicate, and descend/fork (Table 1). Resume and restart keep continuity. Migrate replaces E or S. Evolve changes B. Replicate and descend/fork change who holds authority or identity.
  number: seven operations
  quote: "Table1 separates operations that are often collapsed into “resume” or “fork.”"
  where: Table 1, p2
- Six-phase migration protocol: quiesce+fence, checkpoint, validate, bind, rehydrate, verify+resume. The source stays fenced after the target is activated. It is a single governed promotion point, "not a distributed consensus".
  number: 6 phases, 6 invariants (I1 to I6)
  quote: "After target activation, the source must remain fenced even if it reconnects. This defines a single governed promotion point, not a distributed consensus or automatic cross-host atomic-commit protocol."
  where: Sec 4, p4
- External effects are protected by recording intent with an idempotency key and a fencing epoch before the effect. Providers that offer neither reconciliation nor idempotent delivery must fail closed.
  number: none
  quote: "Before an external effect, the application records intent with an idempotency key and a daemon fencing epoch. A stale process cannot claim or finalize work."
  where: Sec 3.3, p4
- Operational case (B1): one existing agent with nonempty long-term memory moved laptop to desktop and back. It then swapped Codex for Claude Code, then Slack for Telegram. Identity and memory hashes, body revision and 22 historical task IDs were preserved. Outbound and return checkpoints verified 76 and 77 portable files. Authority generations went 8 through 14.
  number: 22 task IDs; 76/77 files; generations 8 to 14
  setup: one agent, author-curated observations from private state, no unfinished task or pending effect injected. Model change was gpt-5.6-sol/high on Codex CLI 0.153.1 to claude-opus-5/high on Claude Code 2.1.258, so model and harness changed together. Twelve Claude probe responses recorded the model ID. Telegram round trip was not tested.
  quote: "the body revision and 22 historical task IDs were preserved. Outbound and return host checkpoints verified 76 and 77 portable files respectively"
  where: Sec 6.1, p6 to p7
- Cross-host task (B1, synthetic, two stages, laptop to desktop): the task paused after stage 1, exported 9 portable files and resumed under the same task ID. Totals were 28 and 28, grand total 56. Both model calls were correct on the first attempt. Attempts went 1 to 2, authority 1 to 2 to 3, and the exported source refused restart.
  number: 9 files; 28+28=56
  setup: Codex CLI 0.153.1, gpt-5.6-sol/high, Python 3.12.14. No tools used. Long-term-memory fixture empty.
  quote: "The target imports nine portable files, verifies and consumes the retained artifact, resumes the same task ID, and computes category totals of 28 and 28, with grand total 56."
  where: Sec 6.2, p7
- Codex to Muse to Codex study (B2, supervised, operator-mediated): 1 qualification run, 5 round trips and 5 same-runtime controls all passed on the first attempt. One planned fault case also completed.
  number: 5/5 round trips; 5/5 controls; 28 continuity checks per round trip plus 18 provenance checks; 13 per control; fault case 28+29 checks
  setup: baseline is the matched same-runtime control with no export or cross-host daemon probe. Codex CLI 0.153.1 configured gpt-6-astra/xhigh. Muse's backend model is unknown. Tasks are simple integer arithmetic. The authors state checks are "assertions, not independent statistical samples".
  quote: "Q and all five ordinary round trips pass on their first attempts, and all five controls pass (Table 5). There are no model-answer retries or unplanned state repairs in this supervised series."
  where: Sec 6.3, p8
- Fenced sources rejected post-export execution without advancing the epoch: 7 migrating source roots and 7 Muse return-export roots.
  number: 7 and 7
  quote: "AllsevenmigratingsourcerootsandsevenMusereturn-export roots reject post-export execution without advancing the authority epoch."
  where: Sec 6.3, p8
- Planned interruption (F): the first Muse worker was killed with SIGKILL (return code -9) before replying. Native recovery paused the same task with the stage-one checkpoint unchanged. A second worker with a fresh nonce completed the task once, and the old nonce was rejected.
  number: one completion; -9
  setup: one prescribed cut while waiting for a reply. It does not test a crash during an external side effect. The exit code 3 for the stale helper is only an operator observation, and the rejection claim rests on retained stderr.
  quote: "Native recovery pauses the same task with its full stage-one checkpoint unchanged. A subsequent worker uses a fresh attempt nonce, completes the task once"
  where: Sec 6.4, p8 to p9
- Mechanism tests: B1 original and anonymized snapshots each passed 963 tests (857 core + 106 provider/library) with no failures or skips. B0 had 833 core + 92 provider/library tests. B2 added 23 adapter tests.
  number: 963; 833+92; 23
  setup: these test implementation mechanisms, not model ability. Totals are not pooled across snapshots.
  quote: "B1’soriginalandanonymizedsnapshotseachpassed963tests, withnofailures or skips"
  where: Sec 5.3, p6; Table 2, p5
- Providers declare a kind, contract version, stable identity and capabilities. There are five kinds: chat, runtime, VCS, review and service (Table 3). A provider swap may reduce capability. A missing capability must fail closed rather than silently select another provider. Capability gain needs authorization.
  number: 5 provider kinds
  quote: "The missing capability must be explicit and must fail closed rather than silently selecting another provider."
  where: Sec 3.1, p3; Table 3, p6; Sec 7.3, p9
- Identity recall is weak evidence. The paper separates mechanical continuity from behavioral identity fidelity.
  number: none
  quote: "an authorized successor may behave differently, while an unauthorized copy may answer identity questions correctly."
  where: Sec 9, p10

LIMITS
- Authors concede: all studies use one evolving Enoch body lineage. The cases are not a controlled all-axis matrix. Claude swaps model and harness together, so a model-only effect is not isolated. Tasks are simple and tool-free. Muse sessions share operator conversation context, so they are not independent. Backend models are not attested. Private B1 data are withheld.
- Authors state the results "do not establish behavioral equivalence, arbitrary-task portability, general exactly-once external effects or unattended reliability."
- Not crash-atomic: SIGKILL bypasses exception rollback, and recovery from every partial-write state is not demonstrated.
- I4 is local only. It does not check remote services (Slack, Telegram) and does not defend against a detached or malicious copy with its own credentials. There is no distributed mutual exclusion.
- Slack to Telegram cursor translation is not demonstrated.
- Open problems: multi-embodiment and merging divergent memory.
- Procedural caveats: the fault package omitted recovery records and logs, which were supplemented from matching hashes. The verifier was adapted after a failed analysis. Criteria and driver were unchanged. Muse token counts were placeholder zeros and were treated as missing.
- Dating: model IDs and tool versions are specific to 2026. Authors own both Enoch and PAI-Bench, a self-evaluation with no external replication.

BUILDS ON
- The authors' prior work: Zhao and Zhao 2026, "Code is the body" (arXiv:2607.28691).
- Distributed systems: Agha 1986 (actors); Bernstein et al. 2014 (Orleans virtual actors); Laadan and Nieh 2007 (checkpoint-restart); Fuggetta, Picco and Vigna 1998 (code mobility); Burckhardt et al. 2021 (durable functions).
- Agent state and continuity: Ravindran 2026 (Portable Agent Memory); He and Yu 2026 (Continuity Kernel).
- Agent architectures: Sumers et al. 2023 (CoALA); Wu et al. 2023 (AutoGen); Park et al. 2023 (Generative Agents); Wang et al. 2023 (Voyager).
- Identity: Perrier and Bennett 2025; Menon 2026.
- Self-evolving systems: MOSS; Autogenesis; SemaClaw; Agent libOS.
- Their own PAI-Bench (arXiv:2609.13637).

CODE: none in the paper. The files body.yaml and self.json are named in Sec 5.1. The Enoch repo is the only code source.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p3): "Runtime-independent agent boundary." It shows P(a) = I, M, B on top and swappable bindings A and B (model, harness, server, surfaces) below. This is the best candidate for the note on what persists versus what is swappable. It also fits a model + loop + tools + memory diagram, though the paper's decomposition differs from that.
- Fig 2 (p4): "Authorized migration." Six boxes (quiesce, checkpoint, validate, bind, rehydrate, verify+resume) with invariants I1 to I6. It is a clear state-machine-style lifecycle.
- Fig 3 (p8): recorded recovery path in F, five steps: request A, SIGKILL, native pause, request B with fresh nonce, complete.
- Table 1 (p2): lifecycle operations. Table 4: invariant-to-evidence map.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Extraction fuses words in places (for example "Qandallfive"). Quotes preserve this where it appears.
- Figure content is text only and I did not view the images.
- The paper is about persistent-agent identity and migration, not the basic agent loop. It does not define an agent as model + loop + tools + memory. It critiques "model + harness" as incomplete. For the note, use it for what state persists across runs and runtimes, and the state-machine and durable-task framing. It does not cover the tool-use loop.
